_lang.name: English
_lang.note: The reference language. Every other file translates these keys. Keep {placeholders} exactly as they are; plural keys hold one text per form the language needs (one, few, many, other...).
group.buildNote: The same offset also appears under {builds}. A game update moves every address, so those are recorded separately: at this offset they are different instructions, not the same bug seen twice.

verdict.repeatFault.one: This exact fault ({fault}) has happened {n} time between {from} and {to}.
verdict.repeatFault.other: This exact fault ({fault}) has happened {n} times between {from} and {to} - it is one repeating problem, not {n} unrelated crashes.

verdict.repeatFaultBuild.one: This exact fault ({fault} on game build {build}) has happened {n} time between {from} and {to}.
verdict.repeatFaultBuild.other: This exact fault ({fault} on game build {build}) has happened {n} times between {from} and {to} - it is one repeating problem, not {n} unrelated crashes.

verdict.ruledOutAll.one: {mods} looked like a lead and was ruled out: the same thing happens in sessions that end normally. Nothing else stands out, so there is no named cause for this one yet.
verdict.ruledOutAll.other: {mods} looked like leads and were ruled out: the same thing happens in sessions that end normally. Nothing else stands out, so there is no named cause for this one yet.

verdict.noModStandsOut: No mod stands out: nothing was logged near the crash that does not also happen in sessions ending normally.
verdict.afterUpdate: This crash happened after the game updated to {version}, before every framework had shown that it runs on that version. See Health.
changes.tooOld: The last session that ended normally before this crash was on {date}, further back than the {days} days of history this scan read, so there is no comparison for it.
verdict.pcDownAfter: The whole PC went down after at least {dur}, not just the game. That is power, overheating or a hard reset, not a mod.
verdict.noRecordAfter: The session ended without any record after at least {dur}: no shutdown, no crash report. The last sign of the game running was at {time}. It was probably closed by force (Task Manager, Alt+F4 during a hang) rather than a crash.
verdict.partialNote: Only the crash report survives for this session; the game's own log from that time has been rotated away, so the play time is unknown.
ev.crashVram: {used} MB of the card's {total} MB were in use ({pct})
ev.crashVramOver: {used} MB of the card's {total} MB were in use ({pct}) — over what the card holds; the driver had spilled into system memory
ev.vramLog: recorded through the session: peak {peak} of the card, median {median}; the last reading was {mb} MB ({pct})
ev.vramLogAbove: recorded through the session: peak {peak} of the card, median {median}, {min} min above 90%; the last reading was {mb} MB ({pct})
ev.settingsChanged: the settings were changed during this session (the game rebuilt its render targets)
verdict.gpuSettingsUnknown: The GPU faulted; the driver reported an error and the engine recorded a GPU crash, not a mod error. The settings file has changed since, so the settings that were running are not known.
verdict.gpuFgRt: The GPU faulted while frame generation and ray tracing ({rtl}) were both on. The engine reported a GPU crash, not a mod error.
verdict.gpuFg: The GPU faulted while frame generation was on. The engine reported a GPU crash, not a mod error.
verdict.gpuRt: The GPU faulted with ray tracing on ({rtl}). The engine reported a GPU crash, not a mod error.
verdict.gpuNone: The GPU faulted with frame generation and ray tracing both off. The engine reported a GPU crash, not a mod error; suspect the driver, temperatures or an overclock.
verdict.gpuVramAt: Video memory was at the card's limit at the time ({used} of {total} MB), which is the usual reason a GPU faults in this game.
verdict.gpuVramOver: Video memory was over the card's limit at the time ({used} of {total} MB), which is the usual reason a GPU faults in this game.
suspect.fgRt.name: Frame generation + ray traced lighting {rtl}
suspect.fg.name: Frame generation
suspect.fg.small: On an {gb} GB card this runs at the video memory ceiling; the map and dense districts push it over.
suspect.fg.why: Frame generation adds its own GPU work and memory on top of everything else.
suspect.gpuHw.name: GPU driver / hardware
suspect.gpuHw.why: No frame generation or ray tracing was on. Try the previous driver, check temperatures, rule out an overclock.
suspect.settingsThen.name: Graphics settings at the time
suspect.settingsThen.why: GPU faults in this game are nearly always frame generation and ray tracing using more video memory than the card has. Check what was on.
verdict.scriptsNotLoaded: The engine stopped because the script files could not be loaded. That is a redscript problem: a broken script mod or a compiler that does not match the game patch.
suspect.redscript.name: redscript / script mods
suspect.redscript.why: The redscript log names the file it choked on.
verdict.hang: The game froze and the engine's watchdog closed it: its main thread had stopped moving for at least {secs} s.
verdict.hangNoTime: The game froze and the engine's watchdog closed it.
verdict.hangRunning: Advanced Crash Reporter found code from {mods} running on the thread that was stuck, so that is the first thing to test.
verdict.hangNoMod: Advanced Crash Reporter found no mod's code running on the thread that was stuck, so nothing here names a mod.
suspect.acrHang: Advanced Crash Reporter found its code running on the thread that was stuck when the game froze. A mod's code on the stuck thread is the strongest lead a freeze leaves.
suspect.acrOverlay: Advanced Crash Reporter found this overlay's code running on that thread. Overlays sit in the game's drawing loop, so this is a lead to test by turning it off, not proof.
verdict.acrModCode: Crashed inside the native code of {mod}: Advanced Crash Reporter found it running on the thread that faulted ({where}).
suspect.acrRunning: Advanced Crash Reporter found its native code running on the thread that faulted ({where}). That is a direct observation, not a correlation: update it or switch it off first.
ev.acrRunning: mod code running on that thread: {mods}
ev.acrNoMod: no mod's code was running on that thread
verdict.winDriver: Windows recorded the fault inside the graphics driver ({module}).
suspect.gpuDriver.name: GPU driver
suspect.gpuDriver.why: The faulting module is the display driver. A clean install of the previous driver version is the usual fix.
verdict.winModDll: Windows recorded the fault inside {module}, which belongs to the mod {mod}.
suspect.nativeCode: Its native code is where the crash happened.
verdict.winGameItself: That is the game itself, which usually means bad data handed to it by a mod (a broken mesh, appearance or sector patch).
verdict.vram: Ran out of video memory. {used} MB of the card's {total} MB were in use when it died ({pct}).
verdict.vramOver: Ran out of video memory. {used} MB of the card's {total} MB were in use when it died ({pct}), past what the card physically holds, so the driver had already spilled into system memory.
verdict.vramBadRead: The engine then failed to get memory for something and crashed reading a resource that was never created ({exception}).
verdict.vramNoError: No driver fault and no mod error was recorded, which is exactly how this looks: the game simply asks for more than the card can hold and falls over.
verdict.vramSettingsChanged: The graphics settings were also changed during this session, minutes before the crash. Rebuilding the render targets is the biggest memory spike a session ever sees, and on an already-full card that alone can end it. Judge the new settings by the next few sessions, not by this one.
suspect.vramCeiling.name: Video memory ceiling
suspect.vramCeiling.levers: The expensive settings right now are {list}. Turning any one of them down frees more than any single mod would.
suspect.vramCeiling.why: Textures and crowd density are the two biggest levers; ray traced lighting and reflections are next.
suspect.texWeight.name: Installed texture weight
suspect.texWeight.why: {size} of mod archives are installed. The heaviest are {list}. Nothing here is broken; it is simply more texture than a {gb} GB card can keep loaded in a dense district.
verdict.scriptError: Script error in {mod} {secs} s before the crash: {text} Not a GPU fault; the engine recorded no error of its own.
verdict.streaming: Crashed during world streaming, {secs} s after ArchiveXL reported a failed sector patch from {mod}.
verdict.streamingShared: {shared} mods were rewriting the map sectors loading around you at the time.

verdict.streamingFailing.one: {shared} mods were rewriting the map sectors loading around you at the time, and {mods} is the one that no longer fits the sector it edits.
verdict.streamingFailing.other: {shared} mods were rewriting the map sectors loading around you at the time, and {mods} are the ones that no longer fit the sectors they edit.

verdict.streamingOne: A world-editing mod is the likely cause.
verdict.partialOnly: A crash was reported at this time. The session log from then has been rotated away, so there is nothing more to go on.
verdict.npcLoading: Crashed while an NPC was loading, with no engine or GPU error recorded. That pattern points at an appearance or body mod for that NPC, or a mod that edits the location.
verdict.sectorPatch: Crashed while a world sector patch was being applied during streaming. That points at a mod that edits the map in that area.
verdict.pcDown: The whole PC went down, not just the game. That is power, overheating or a hard reset, not a mod.
verdict.noRecord: The session ended without any record: no shutdown, no crash report. The game was probably closed by force (Task Manager, Alt+F4 during a hang) or the PC was restarted.
verdict.nothingLogged: Crashed with nothing logged in the two minutes before. The engine could not describe it, no mod reported an error, and the driver did not fault.
verdict.districtCluster: This is crash number {n} in {district}; something specific to that area is likely.
suspect.worldPatch: Edits world sectors; failed or overlapping sector patches crash during streaming.
area.failing: ArchiveXL reported this mod's patch did not fit the sector it was applied to during this session.
area.shared: Shares these sectors with several other mods.
suspect.location: Its patches rewrite {where} ({n} references). With several mods editing one place, one of them is the usual cause of a crash while NPCs or the area load.
suspect.locationWip: Its patches rewrite {where} ({n} references), and it is an unfinished early version. With several mods editing one place, one of them is the usual cause of a crash while NPCs or the area load.

suspect.areaFailing.one: It rewrites {sectors} of the map sectors that were loading around you, and ArchiveXL had to skip part of its patch this session because the sector no longer matches what the mod expects. {n} other mod edits the same ground.
suspect.areaFailing.other: It rewrites {sectors} of the map sectors that were loading around you, and ArchiveXL had to skip part of its patch this session because the sector no longer matches what the mod expects. {n} other mods edit the same ground.

suspect.areaShared.one: It rewrites {sectors} of the map sectors that were loading around you, shared with {n} other mod. Overlapping sector edits are a common cause of crashes while moving through an area.
suspect.areaShared.other: It rewrites {sectors} of the map sectors that were loading around you, shared with {n} other mods. Overlapping sector edits are a common cause of crashes while moving through an area.

ruled.brokenPlugin: It errors constantly because its native plugin will not load on this game patch. That is a standing fault, not something that happened at the crash.
suspect.scriptErr: Its script errored {secs} s before the crash: {text}

suspect.notInClean.one: It does not do this in the {n} session that ended cleanly.
suspect.notInClean.other: It does not do this in any of the {n} sessions that ended cleanly.

suspect.xlErr: ArchiveXL reported a problem with its patch {secs} s before the crash: {text}
suspect.noBaseline0: No session on record has ended cleanly, so there is nothing to compare this against. Treat it as a lead, not a finding.

suspect.noBaselineFew.one: Only {n} session on record ended cleanly, which is too few to rule anything out. Treat this as a lead, not a finding.
suspect.noBaselineFew.other: Only {n} sessions on record ended cleanly, which is too few to rule anything out. Treat this as a lead, not a finding.

health.noClean.title: No session has ended cleanly yet
health.oneClean.title: Only one session has ended cleanly
health.noClean.detail: Crash Doctor rules a mod out by checking whether it misbehaves in sessions that end normally too. With no clean sessions on record there is nothing to compare against, so every suspect below is a lead rather than a finding. Play until you quit the game normally a couple of times and scan again: the diagnosis gets sharper, not vaguer, the more you play.
health.oneClean.detail: Crash Doctor rules a mod out by checking whether it misbehaves in sessions that end normally too. With one clean session on record there is nothing to compare against, so every suspect below is a lead rather than a finding. Play until you quit the game normally a couple of times and scan again: the diagnosis gets sharper, not vaguer, the more you play.

health.baseline.title.one: {n} clean session is being used to rule things out
health.baseline.title.other: {n} clean sessions are being used to rule things out

health.baseline.detail: Anything that also happens in a session you quit normally cannot be why another one crashed. Of the {total} sessions whose logs the game still keeps, {clean} ended cleanly and {crashed} crashed. That comparison is what lets the diagnosis discard background noise instead of blaming it. Older sessions are remembered, but their logs have been rotated away, so they cannot be compared.
health.week.kinds: GPU faults: {gpu}. Out of video memory: {vram}. Mod or script: {script}. Froze: {hang}. Other: {other}.

health.week.partial.one: Plus {n} crash report from a session whose logs have been rotated away.
health.week.partial.other: Plus {n} crash reports from sessions whose logs have been rotated away.

health.groups.detail.one: {crashes}: {n} distinct fault. Crashes at the same machine instruction are the same bug.
health.groups.detail.other: {crashes} fall into {n} distinct faults. Crashes at the same machine instruction are the same bug.

health.groups.noneLive: None of them has happened since your last clean session, so nothing is currently recurring.

health.groups.live.other: {n} are still happening since the last clean session.

health.groups.titleOne: All your crashes are one repeating fault

health.groups.titleAllDifferent.other: Your {n} crashes are {n} different faults, none of them repeating

health.groups.title: Your crashes are {groups} separate problems, not {total} random ones
health.injector.title: {tool} was running inside the game in {n} of these crashes
health.injector.detail: Tools like this patch game code at fixed addresses, so one built for a different game version writes into the wrong place. That makes it worth knowing about, but {n} of {total} is a correlation, not a cause, and it can only be settled by playing without it. Close it before launching if you want to test that.
health.frameworksClean.title: Frameworks loaded cleanly

health.frameworksClean.detail.one: RED4ext {version} and {n} native plugin loaded without warnings; scripts compiled.
health.frameworksClean.detail.other: RED4ext {version} and {n} native plugins loaded without warnings; scripts compiled.

health.unread.title: Some sources could not be read
settings.fgRt.title: Frame generation and ray tracing together
settings.fgRt.detail: On {gb} GB this is the combination behind GPU faults. Drop ray traced lighting to Medium or turn frame generation off.
settings.heldUp.title: These settings have held up
settings.heldUp.detail: The longest clean session since this settings file was written ran {dur}.
settings.written.title: Settings file last written
settings.written.detail: {date}. Verdicts only quote settings for crashes that happened after this time.

update.fw.notStarted: {name} has not started since the update, although the game has run: it may not support this game version yet.
update.fw.notRun: {name}: the game has not been started since the update, so there is nothing to read yet.
update.fw.red4extErrors: RED4ext {version} started on {date} and reported an error: "{line}"

update.fw.red4extRan.one: RED4ext {version} started on game {game} and loaded {n} plugin.
update.fw.red4extRan.other: RED4ext {version} started on game {game} and loaded {n} plugins.

update.fw.pluginAbsent: {name} is installed but did not load.

update.fw.otherPlugins.one: RED4ext also refused {n} other native plugin on this version: {list}.
update.fw.otherPlugins.other: RED4ext also refused {n} other native plugins on this version: {list}.

update.fw.cetRefused: Cyber Engine Tweaks said it does not support this game version: "{line}"
update.fw.cetRan: Cyber Engine Tweaks {version} started on game build {game}.

update.fw.redscriptErrors.one: redscript compiled with {n} error since the update: {text}
update.fw.redscriptErrors.other: redscript compiled with {n} errors since the update, the first: {text}

update.fw.redscriptRan: redscript compiled the scripts without errors.
update.titleProblems: Your game updated to {version}, and your frameworks do not all support it yet
update.titleFine: Your game updated to {version}, and your frameworks loaded on it
update.titleChanged: Your game changed back to {version} (it was {from})
update.why: RED4ext, redscript, Cyber Engine Tweaks, ArchiveXL, TweakXL and Codeware hook into the game's own code, so after a game update they usually need an update of their own before the mods built on them work again. Until they support {version}, crashes at start-up and mods that silently do nothing are expected, and they are not a sign that your mods are broken.
update.said: What their logs say since the update: {list}
update.noFrameworks: No mod framework is installed, so the update should not affect your mods.
update.adviceBad: Wait for the frameworks that refused or have not started to release a version for {version} (their Nexus pages say when), rather than reinstalling or disabling mods one by one. Playing without mods until then is the safe choice.
update.adviceWaiting: Start the game once and scan again: each framework writes in its log whether it runs on the new version.
update.adviceFine: Every framework Crash Doctor found has run on the new version without complaint.
rule.enabler.title: A DLSS/FSR enabler has replaced files the game now owns
rule.enabler.detail: Found {files} in the game folder. Since patch 2.3 the game ships its own FidelityFX and XeSS, and these tools overwrite those DLLs with their own copies. That combination is a common cause of GPU faults and of the game refusing to start after an update. Removing the mod does not undo it, because the game's original files were replaced: verify the game files through Steam, GOG or Epic to put them back.

rule.emptyArchive.title.one: One mod archive is empty or truncated
rule.emptyArchive.title.other: {n} mod archives are empty or truncated

rule.emptyArchive.detail: {list}. A real archive is never this small: these are interrupted downloads. Nothing will report an error; the content simply is not there, and the game can fault where it was expected. Re-download and reinstall these mods.
rule.cloudSaves.title: Your saves are inside a cloud-synced folder
rule.cloudSaves.detail: Saves are at {path}. Sync clients rewrite files while the game is writing them, and can leave a save as an online-only placeholder that is not really on disk. That shows up as corrupted saves and as crashes on load. Move the Cyberpunk 2077 save folder out of the synced area, or exclude it from syncing.
rule.overlay.title: {tool} was injected into the game in {n} of {total} crashes
rule.overlay.detail: Tools that hook the game's rendering sit between it and the driver, and this one is a documented source of instability with heavily modded Cyberpunk. {n} of {total} is a correlation and not a cause: the way to settle it is to close it and play.

rule.oom.title.one: The engine ran out of memory in {n} crash
rule.oom.title.other: The engine ran out of memory in {n} crashes

rule.oom.lead.one: The crash report carries the engine's own out-of-memory flag in {count} of {n} crash, most recently on {date}.
rule.oom.lead.other: The crash report carries the engine's own out-of-memory flag in {count} of {n} crashes, most recently on {date}.

rule.oom.meaning: That is the engine recording that it asked the system for memory and did not get it.
rule.oom.unmeasured: None of those crashes recorded how much video memory was in use, so there is no way to tell from here whether the card was the thing that ran out.
rule.oom.cardFull: In all {n} of them the graphics card was also at 95% or more, so this is the same problem the video memory reading already describes: the card is the constraint, and the settings that free the most are textures and crowd density.
rule.oom.cardFine: In {n} of them the card was below its ceiling, as low as {pct}, so the card is not what ran out there. Something else is: the Windows page file (a small or disabled one is the usual cause on a machine with plenty of RAM), other programs holding memory, or simply the number of mod archives the engine has to keep indexed.
rule.oom.ram: This machine has {gb} GB of RAM, which does not help if the page file is capped: Windows still refuses the allocation.
rule.oom.ramUnknown: Having a lot of RAM does not help if the page file is capped: Windows still refuses the allocation.
rule.stack.titleAll: All {n} of your crashes are stack overflows

rule.stack.title.one: {n} of {total} crashes is a stack overflow

rule.stack.lead: The stack ran out of room.
rule.stack.leadWhere: The stack ran out of room, faulting in {modules}.
rule.stack.meaning: A stack only runs out when something calls itself without ever returning, so this is a loop in code: not the graphics card, not video memory, and not something a settings change will alter. In this game it is nearly always scripts: two mods replacing the same method so that each one ends up calling the other.

rule.stack.wrapped.one: redscript reported {n} method being replaced more than once this session, which is exactly the shape that produces it. Those warnings name the methods, and the mods replacing them are where to look first.
rule.stack.wrapped.other: redscript reported {n} methods being replaced more than once this session, which is exactly the shape that produces it. Those warnings name the methods, and the mods replacing them are where to look first.

rule.stack.noWrapped: Start with whatever was installed or updated most recently, and look for two mods that change the same thing.

rule.startup.title.one: Your {n} recent crash happened in the first {min} minutes
rule.startup.title.other: All {n} recent crashes happened in the first {min} minutes

rule.startup.meaning: A crash that always arrives before you are properly in the game is a loading problem (a plugin, a script that fails to compile, or a save that cannot be read) rather than anything about where you were or what you were doing.

rule.startup.played.one: {n} session in the same period got past that point and ended normally, so the game is not broken outright.
rule.startup.played.other: {n} sessions in the same period got past that point and ended normally, so the game is not broken outright.

rule.startup.easy: It is also the easiest kind of crash to find, because it happens every time instead of eventually: Find it will narrow the mod list down in a handful of short runs rather than a week of playing. Start with whatever you installed or updated most recently.
rule.vortexMissing.titleOne: Vortex thinks {mod} is installed, but its files are not in the game folder

rule.vortexMissing.titleMany.one: {n} file Vortex deployed is missing from the game folder
rule.vortexMissing.titleMany.other: {n} files Vortex deployed are missing from the game folder

rule.vortexMissing.none.one: The {n} file in Vortex's deployment record is not actually on disk.
rule.vortexMissing.none.other: None of the {n} files in Vortex's deployment record is actually on disk.

rule.vortexMissing.some.one: {missing} of the {n} file in Vortex's deployment record is not on disk, across {mods}: {list}.
rule.vortexMissing.some.other: {missing} of the {n} files in Vortex's deployment record are not on disk, across {mods}: {list}.

rule.vortexMissing.why: Verifying the game files through Steam, GOG or Epic does this: the store deletes everything it does not recognise, and the manager is never told. Antivirus quarantine and a deployment that was interrupted have the same effect.
rule.vortexMissing.fix: Vortex still lists these mods as installed and the game never sees them, which is the state behind "the mod does nothing" and ArchiveXL complaining that a file does not exist. Open Vortex and deploy again; purge first if it says everything is already deployed.

rule.vortexMissing.skipped.one: ({n} further file deploys to its own target folder and was not checked.)
rule.vortexMissing.skipped.other: ({n} further files deploy to their own target folder and were not checked.)

rule.mo2Missing.titleOne: Mod Organizer 2 has {mod} enabled, but its folder is missing

rule.mo2Missing.titleMany.one: {n} mod is enabled in Mod Organizer 2 but its folder is missing
rule.mo2Missing.titleMany.other: {n} mods are enabled in Mod Organizer 2 but their folders are missing

rule.mo2Missing.detail: The profile "{profile}" enables {list}, but there is no folder for them in {folder}, so the game gets none of their files. That happens when a mod folder is deleted or renamed outside Mod Organizer 2, or when the mods folder moves. Refresh Mod Organizer 2 (F5) and reinstall what it marks as missing.

rule.mo2Hidden.title.one: {winner} hides {n} script or plugin file of {loser} in Mod Organizer 2
rule.mo2Hidden.title.other: {winner} hides {n} script or plugin files of {loser} in Mod Organizer 2

rule.mo2Hidden.detail: Both mods ship {files}. Mod Organizer 2 gives the game one copy of each file, here {winner}'s, because it has the higher priority, so the copies from {loser} never load. That is usually intended (a patch, or an update installed as a separate mod); it is worth knowing if {loser} seems to do nothing.
rule.plugin.title: Native plugin refuses to load on this patch: {name}
rule.plugin.detail: {line} Whatever this mod does through its native half is silently off, and its script half may error.
rule.xl.titleWorld: World sector patch fails every launch
rule.xl.titleMissing: Mod points at resources that do not exist
rule.xl.world: Another mod changed that sector first, or the game patch did; the patch is skipped.
rule.xl.missing: The mod references files that are not installed or were removed in a game patch; those parts are skipped.
rule.rs.overwriteTitle: Two mods replace the same script method
rule.rs.errorTitle: redscript error: a script mod does not compile

rule.spam.title.other: {mod} logs the same error {n} times per session

rule.spam.detail: {text} A feature of the mod is not working; check for an update.
rule.dupScript.detail: Identical copies of one script compile more than once; the compiler warns and the last one wins. Two mods are bundling the same fix: {list}

rule.vramCrash.title.one: Video memory at the last crash
rule.vramCrash.title.other: Video memory at the last {n} crashes

rule.vramCrash.none.other: None of the last {n} crashes was short of video memory, so the card is not the constraint.

rule.vramCrash.some.one: The last crash happened with the {total} MB card at 95% or more. That is where allocations start failing, and a failed allocation crashes the engine with nothing written to any log.
rule.vramCrash.some.other: {hit} of the last {n} crashes happened with the {total} MB card at 95% or more. That is where allocations start failing, and a failed allocation crashes the engine with nothing written to any log.

rule.vram.levers: Textures and crowd density free the most; ray traced lighting and reflections are next.

rule.vramPlay.title.one: Video memory while you played, last session
rule.vramPlay.title.other: Video memory while you played, last {n} sessions

rule.vramPlay.none.one: In the last recorded session the {total} MB card never sat near its ceiling, so video memory is not the constraint with the current settings.
rule.vramPlay.none.other: In the last {n} recorded sessions the {total} MB card never sat near its ceiling, so video memory is not the constraint with the current settings.

rule.vramPlay.hot.one: In the last recorded session the {total} MB card ran close to full, touching 95% or more. That is the range where the engine's next texture or mesh allocation can fail, and a failed allocation crashes it with nothing written to any log.
rule.vramPlay.hot.other: In {hot} of the last {n} recorded sessions the {total} MB card ran close to full, touching 95% or more. That is the range where the engine's next texture or mesh allocation can fail, and a failed allocation crashes it with nothing written to any log.

rule.vramPlay.hotAbove.one: In the last recorded session the {total} MB card ran close to full, {min} min above 90%. That is the range where the engine's next texture or mesh allocation can fail, and a failed allocation crashes it with nothing written to any log.
rule.vramPlay.hotAbove.other: In {hot} of the last {n} recorded sessions the {total} MB card ran close to full, {min} min above 90% in all. That is the range where the engine's next texture or mesh allocation can fail, and a failed allocation crashes it with nothing written to any log.

rule.fgRt.title: Frame generation with ray tracing on an {gb} GB GPU
rule.fgRt.detail: Ray traced lighting is {rtl}. This combination sits at the video memory ceiling on {gb} GB; GPU faults on the map or in dense areas are the usual result. Turn one of them down.
rule.pt.title: Path tracing on a card with 12 GB or less
rule.pt.detail: Path tracing needs more video memory than any other setting. Expect faults in dense areas.
rule.driver.title: Graphics driver is from {date}
rule.driver.detail: Not necessarily a problem, but frame generation and ray tracing fixes ship in driver updates.
gfx.noteDynamic: Depends on your monitor and graphics card, so it is set in the game. A profile saves and restores it as the game wrote it.
prof.tooLong: That name is too long; keep it under 60 characters.

prof.gameRunning: Close Cyberpunk 2077 first. The game rewrites its settings file when it exits, so a change made while it is running would be undone.
prof.cannotRead: Could not read the game's settings file.

prof.applied.other: Applied "{name}": {n} settings changed. Start the game to use it. The previous settings are backed up; Undo puts them back.

dump.read: The game tried to read memory that was not there any more, typically a resource that failed to load or was freed while still in use.
dump.write: The game tried to write to memory it did not own.
dump.invalid: The game touched memory that was not valid.
dump.breakpoint: The engine stopped itself deliberately: it hit a condition it treats as fatal rather than carrying on.
dump.stack: The stack ran out of room, usually endless recursion in a script or a mod calling itself.
dump.page: A page of memory could not be read from disk. Suspect the drive or a damaged game file.

elim.ruledOut.one: It logs the same thing in {n} session that ended perfectly normally. Something that happens when nothing goes wrong cannot be why something went wrong.
elim.ruledOut.other: It logs the same thing in {n} sessions that ended perfectly normally. Something that happens when nothing goes wrong cannot be why something went wrong.

elim.ruledOutBoth.one: It logs the same thing in {n} session that ended perfectly normally, as well as {crashed} that crashed. Something that happens when nothing goes wrong cannot be why something went wrong.
elim.ruledOutBoth.other: It logs the same thing in {n} sessions that ended perfectly normally, as well as {crashed} that crashed. Something that happens when nothing goes wrong cannot be why something went wrong.

upd.noAnswer: The check did not get an answer: {error}

logs.none: There are no logs to clear.

logs.failedSome.one: Could not clear the logs: {error} {n} was already moved to {folder} and can be put back.
logs.failedSome.other: Could not clear the logs: {error} {n} were already moved to {folder} and can be put back.

logs.noneMoved: None of the logs could be moved. Another program may have them open.

logs.moved.one: Moved {n} log out of the game's log folders.
logs.moved.other: Moved {n} logs out of the game's log folders.

logs.skipped.one: {n} could not be moved and was left.
logs.skipped.other: {n} could not be moved and were left.

logs.nothingBack: There is nothing to put back.

logs.keptNewer.other: {n} stayed in {folder} because the game has written a newer file with the same name.

warn.vortexAndMo2: Both Vortex and Mod Organizer 2 ({folder}) manage this game. Crash Doctor read Vortex's list, because Vortex deploys into the game folder itself. To read Mod Organizer 2's list instead, put its folder in "Mo2Path" in Crash Doctor's config.json.
bisect.noTimed: No crash of this fault has a known length (their session logs were gone before they were scanned), so {min} minutes is a floor rather than a measurement. Treat a clean run as weak evidence until a timed crash exists.

bisect.basis.one: twice the typical {median} min this fault takes to appear, from {n} timed crash
bisect.basis.other: twice the typical {median} min this fault takes to appear, from {n} timed crashes

bisect.basisRough.one: twice the {median} min the only timed crash of this fault took, so treat it as rough
bisect.basisRough.other: twice the {median} min the {n} timed crashes of this fault took, so treat it as rough

bisect.capped: Capped at {max} min. Uncapped it would be {raw} min ({basis}). A fault this slow to appear makes a clean run weaker evidence than usual, so give the step more than one session where you can.
bisect.floor: {min} min is the floor; {basis} would give only {raw}.

bisect.recurred.one: The same fault happened again on {date} with that {n} mod off, so it is not the cause.
bisect.recurred.other: The same fault happened again on {date} with those {n} mods off, so none of them is the cause.

bisect.survived.one: You played {n} minute cleanly on {date} with those mods off, longer than this fault normally takes. It is most likely one of them.
bisect.survived.other: You played {n} minutes cleanly on {date} with those mods off, longer than this fault normally takes. It is most likely one of them.

bisect.foundHow.one: Narrowed from {mods} mods in {n} test, by watching whether {signature} came back each time.
bisect.foundHow.other: Narrowed from {mods} mods in {n} tests, by watching whether {signature} came back each time.

bisect.foundNext: Now turn all the other mods back on in {manager} and leave only {mod} off. If the fault stays away with everything else running, that is your answer. If it comes back, the cause was a combination rather than one mod, and the run has to start again with that one excluded.
bisect.exhausted: The cause is not among the mods that were tested.
bisect.exhaustedDetail: Every candidate was cleared, so this fault comes from something else: the game itself, a driver, hardware, or a tool running alongside the game. Check the Health page for anything injected into the process. Turn your mods back on in {manager}; none of them was responsible.
bisect.stale: The game updated, so this hunt cannot continue.
bisect.staleWhy: Every round so far was measured against game build {build}, and an update moves every address: the fault being hunted ({fault}) cannot happen at that address any more.

bisect.staleNext.one: Nothing learned in {n} round is wrong, but it cannot be carried forward. Turn your mods back on, play until the crash reappears, then start a new hunt against whatever fault the new build reports.
bisect.staleNext.other: Nothing learned in {n} rounds is wrong, but it cannot be carried forward. Turn your mods back on, play until the crash reappears, then start a new hunt against whatever fault the new build reports.

bisect.setUp.one: Step {index}: turn off {off} of the {n} mod still in the running.
bisect.setUp.other: Step {index}: turn off {off} of the {n} mods still in the running.

bisect.stillOff.one: {n} that must stay in the test is currently disabled and needs turning back on.
bisect.stillOff.other: {n} that must stay in the test are currently disabled and need turning back on.

bisect.doIt: Do it in {manager}, deploy, then scan again: Crash Doctor checks what is actually deployed rather than taking your word for it.
bisect.doItMo2: Untick them in Mod Organizer 2's mod list, then scan again: Crash Doctor reads the profile's mod list itself rather than taking your word for it.
bisect.ready: Step {index} is set up correctly. Go and play.

bisect.readyDetail.one: Play the way you normally do, in the place this fault usually happens. Either it comes back, which clears this {n} mod, or you get a clean run of at least {min} minutes, which points at it. Then scan again; the result is read from your logs automatically.
bisect.readyDetail.other: Play the way you normally do, in the place this fault usually happens. Either it comes back, which clears all {n} of these, or you get a clean run of at least {min} minutes, which points at them. Then scan again; the result is read from your logs automatically.

bisect.running: Step {index} is running. Play, then scan.

bisect.runningDetail.one: Nothing decisive yet. A crash with {signature} clears this {n} mod; a clean run of {min}+ minutes points at it. Anything shorter is not conclusive either way, so keep playing.
bisect.runningDetail.other: Nothing decisive yet. A crash with {signature} clears these {n} mods; a clean run of {min}+ minutes points at them. Anything shorter is not conclusive either way, so keep playing.

host.includeMods:
Include your mod list in the saved report?

It names all {n} of your mods. That is usually what makes a report worth reading, but saved reports often get posted publicly, so it is worth deciding on purpose.

Leaving it out also removes mod names from the requirements and area panels. The handful of mods the diagnosis actually names still appear, because naming them is the diagnosis.

Yes - include the mod list.   No - leave it out.   Cancel - do not save.

The mod's original file will be put back.

Crash Doctor will ask you to switch groups of mods off in {manager}, play, and scan again. It never changes anything itself: it only checks what is actually enabled and reads the result from your logs.

{mods} mods are in the running, so expect about {n} round of play.

ui.area.rewriting.other: {n} mods were rewriting them as they loaded.

ui.ok.allClean.other: {n} sessions on record, every one closed normally.

ui.bisect.lead: When the logs name nothing, this always works. Crash Doctor asks you to switch off half the mods, you play, and it watches whether the same fault comes back, then halves again. It never changes a mod itself: it tells you what to switch off in {manager} and then checks what is actually enabled before it will trust the result.
ui.bisect.none: No fault has happened more than once yet, so there is nothing worth bisecting. Come back if a crash starts repeating: chasing a one-off costs days and usually proves nothing.

ui.prof.noFile: The game's settings file was not found. Launch Cyberpunk 2077 once so it creates one, then scan again.
ui.prof.running: Cyberpunk 2077 is running. You can save and edit profiles, but close the game before applying one: it rewrites its settings when it exits, which would undo the change.
ui.prof.playTip: Back up your settings, put this profile in, start the game, and put your settings back when it closes
ui.prof.updateTip: Replace this profile with what the game is set to now
ui.prof.saveCurrentHelp: Keeps everything the game is set to now under a name, so you can switch back to it in one click.
ui.prof.backedUp: Your settings from before the last change were backed up {when}.
ui.prof.explain: Play with this backs up your settings, puts the profile in, starts the game, and puts your settings back when it closes. Apply leaves the profile in until you change it, and Undo puts the previous settings back. Only graphics and display settings are touched, never controls, audio or key bindings.
ui.prof.nameFirst: Give the profile a name first.
ui.saved.onlyReport: Only the crash report was left: the session's own logs had already been rotated away by the game.
ui.saved.copyKept: A copy of this crash's logs is kept, so it can still be compared after the game deletes them.
ui.saved.off: Crash logs are not being kept. Turn it on under Settings to save a copy of each crash before the game deletes its logs.
ui.arch.title: Keep a copy of every crash's logs
ui.arch.help: The game deletes its logs after a few launches, which is how most crashes end up with nothing left to examine. Crash Doctor zips the crash report and that session's logs the first time it sees a crash, and keeps the three most recent clean sessions to compare against. It only copies; nothing in the game folder changes.
ui.logs.title: Clear old logs
ui.logs.help: Moves the logs written by the game's mod frameworks (RED4ext and its plugins, Cyber Engine Tweaks, redscript) out of the game folder, so the next launch starts with fresh ones. Nothing is deleted: they go into Crash Doctor's own folder and can be put back. Crash reports are left alone. Close the game first.
ui.logs.mo2: With Mod Organizer 2, the same logs are moved out of its overwrite folder too, and put back there.

ui.logs.inGame.other: {n} logs in the game's log folders, {size}.

ui.vcard.title: Record video memory while the game runs
ui.vcard.help: The game only writes how full the card was into crash reports, so a session that did not crash leaves no number at all. While this window is open, Crash Doctor reads the same Windows counters Task Manager uses (NVIDIA, AMD and Intel alike) every 5 seconds and keeps one small file per launch, then shows each session's peak, median and time above 90%. Nothing runs after the window is closed, and the game is never touched. When the game closes, the scan runs again by itself.
ui.vcard.none: Nothing recorded yet. Leave this window open while you play.

ui.toast.vramOff: Video memory will not be recorded. Files already saved are left where they are.

ui.upd.title: Tell me when a newer version is out
ui.upd.help: Off by default, because everything else in Crash Doctor stays on your PC. When it is on, the app fetches one small version file at most once a day and compares it with this build ({v}). Nothing about you or your install is sent, and it never downloads or installs anything itself: a newer version is a line at the top of the window and a button that opens the download page.

ui.report.summaryHelp: Copy summary is the one to paste for help: plain text, short enough for a mod's Bugs tab, a forum post or a Discord message.
ui.report.aiHelp: Copy for an AI builds the same evidence into a question you can paste into Claude, ChatGPT or any assistant you already use. Crash Doctor gathers things no chatbot can see on its own (the faulting instruction, the video memory at the moment of death, and what the sessions that ended normally have already ruled out), so handing those over is worth far more than describing the crash from memory. It also asks the assistant not to invent mod names. Nothing is sent anywhere by Crash Doctor; it only puts text on your clipboard.
ui.report.htmlHelp: Save full report as HTML writes one self-contained file (every session, every crash, the whole health list) that opens in any browser. When the window is not in English, the file carries an English copy as well, one click away. Most help pages will not let you attach a file, so it is for somewhere that does, for a Crash Doctor bug report, or as your own before-and-after record when you change a setting or switch a mod off.
ui.report.privacy: None of them contains personal data beyond your game path and hardware, and folder paths under your Windows account are replaced first.
ui.copiedAi: Copied. Paste it into Claude, ChatGPT or whatever you use.
ui.noClipboard: Could not reach the clipboard. Select the text below and copy it.
ui.selectCopy: Select the text and copy it.

ui.ai.intro1: You are helping me work out why my heavily modded Cyberpunk 2077 keeps crashing.
ui.ai.intro2: Everything below was measured by a tool called Crash Doctor, which reads the crash dumps, the mod loaders' logs and the Windows event log on this PC. It is evidence rather than my recollection, so the numbers and timings are accurate and you can reason from them directly.

ui.ai.rule1: Do not invent mod names, versions or file paths. If you name a mod, it has to be one that appears above.
ui.ai.rule2: If the evidence does not support a conclusion, say so plainly. "I do not know, here is what would tell us" is a useful answer; a confident guess is not.
ui.ai.rule3: Correlation is not cause. If something appears in my crashes but also in the sessions that ended normally, it has been ruled out above and is noise.
ui.ai.rule4: Prefer one concrete next test over a list of possibilities, and tell me what result would confirm it and what result would rule it out.
ui.ai.rule5: I can disable mods, change settings and reinstall things. I cannot recompile anything.
ui.ai.question: My question: based on this evidence, what is the most likely cause, and what single thing should I test next?

kb.archivexl-sector-node-mismatch.title: A world-editing mod expects a map that the game patch changed
kb.archivexl-sector-node-mismatch.says: ArchiveXL world patches address map objects by position in a list. A game update, or another mod editing the same sector first, shifts that list, so the patch is aimed at the wrong object and ArchiveXL skips it. The part of the mod that edits the world is simply not applied from then on.
kb.archivexl-sector-node-mismatch.do: Check whether the mod has an update for your game patch. If it is the newest version, the sector is being changed by something else first - the area panel on the diagnosis shows which other mods patch the same sector.
kb.archivexl-sector-node-mismatch.source: ArchiveXL's own message, and seen repeatedly on the reference install after patch 2.31
kb.cet-nil-global.title: A Lua mod is calling into its native half, which is not there
kb.cet-nil-global.says: A Cyber Engine Tweaks mod is calling a function that does not exist. The usual reason is that the mod ships two halves - a Lua part and a native plugin - and the native half was refused by RED4ext because it was built for a different game patch. The Lua half keeps running and keeps calling functions that never loaded, often every few seconds for the whole session.
kb.cet-nil-global.do: Check the Requirements screen and the Health list for a plugin that refused to load. If one is named, that mod needs an update for your patch; until then the feature is off whatever the Lua side does.
kb.cet-nil-global.source: Lua's own error text; the pairing with a refused native plugin was confirmed on the reference install
kb.resource-does-not-exist.title: A mod points at a file that is not installed
kb.resource-does-not-exist.says: The mod refers to a game resource by path and that path is not there. Either part of the mod did not install (a missing requirement, or an archive that downloaded incompletely), or a game patch moved or removed the file. The loader skips that part and carries on, so the mod appears installed while some of it does nothing.
kb.resource-does-not-exist.do: Check the mod's requirements - a missing dependency is the most common cause - and reinstall it if the Health list also reports an empty or truncated archive.
kb.nvlddmkm-tdr.title: Windows reset the graphics driver
kb.nvlddmkm-tdr.says: Windows decided the graphics card had stopped responding and reset the driver underneath the game. That is a hardware or driver level event, not a mod one - no mod can cause it directly, though running the card at its limit makes it far more likely. The game almost always dies with it.
kb.nvlddmkm-tdr.do: Reduce whatever is loading the card hardest, and check the video memory reading on this crash. If it happens with the card comfortable, try the previous driver version and check temperatures.
kb.nvlddmkm-tdr.source: Windows event log; nvlddmkm event 153 is the NVIDIA timeout-detection-and-recovery event
kb.gpu-crash-unknown-reasons.title: The engine's own "Gpu Crash for unknown reasons" message
kb.gpu-crash-unknown-reasons.says: This is the engine saying a DirectX call failed and that it has nothing useful to add - its own message admits the callstack is probably irrelevant. It means the graphics work the game asked for did not complete. The cause is almost never in this message; it is in what the card was being asked to do.
kb.gpu-crash-unknown-reasons.do: Read the video memory figure for this crash first. If the card was near its limit, that is the lead. If it was not, check the Windows driver events on the same timestamp.
kb.gpu-crash-unknown-reasons.source: the engine's own text, quoted verbatim in the crash report
kb.stack-overflow-recursion.title: Stack overflow means something called itself forever
kb.stack-overflow-recursion.says: The stack only runs out when code calls itself without ever returning. It is a logic fault, never hardware and never video memory, and no graphics setting changes it. In this game it is nearly always scripts - most often two mods wrapping the same function so that each ends up calling the other.
kb.stack-overflow-recursion.do: Look at what was installed or updated most recently, and at any redscript warning about an annotation being overwritten: those name the function two mods are both replacing.
kb.stack-overflow-recursion.source: the Windows exception code, and the usual cause in a scripted game
kb.access-violation-null.title: The game read from an address that was never valid
kb.access-violation-null.says: The address the game tried to read is very close to zero, which means it was handed nothing where it expected an object. Something asked for a thing that had not been created, or had already been destroyed. Where this follows a mod loading or unloading something, that is the place to look.
kb.access-violation-null.do: Check what the evidence shows in the seconds before the crash, and whether this fault repeats. A fault that repeats at the same address is one problem and worth a bisect; a one-off usually is not.
kb.access-violation-null.source: standard interpretation of a low-address access violation

verdict.repeatHang.one: The game has frozen this way {n} time between {from} and {to}.
verdict.repeatHang.other: The game has frozen this way {n} times between {from} and {to}. The engine's watchdog ends every freeze at the same place, so this says the game keeps freezing, not that every freeze has the same cause.

known.old: {name} {installed} is older than {needed}, the first {name} release for game {game} ({date}). Update it to {needed} or newer.
known.oldNoDate: {name} {installed} is older than {needed}, the first {name} release for game {game}. Update it to {needed} or newer.
known.noRelease: {name} {installed} was built for game {built}, and there was no {name} release for {game} yet when this version of Crash Doctor was made ({date}); its Nexus page says when there is one.
plugin.refusedPlain: In plain words: {name} {version} was built for game build {runtime}, and RED4ext does not start a plugin on a game build it was not built for. It is switched off, not broken, until its author releases a version for your game.
update.fw.pluginDiedLoading: The game closed while RED4ext was loading {name}: RED4ext's log stops at "Loading plugin … {name}.dll" with nothing after it. A native plugin built for an older game version can take the game down like this on a new one, seconds after it starts.
update.adviceKnown: Update the frameworks that already have a release for {version}, named above. For the others, wait for their releases rather than reinstalling or disabling mods one by one; playing without mods until then is the safe choice.
update.sources: What each framework wrote in its own log comes first. The release versions named here come from the frameworks' own release notes, checked up to {date}; a newer release may be out since.
update.leadRecent: Your game is {version}, the update released on {date}.
verdict.diedLoading: The game closed {secs} s after it started, while RED4ext was loading the native plugin {name}: RED4ext's log stops at "Loading plugin … {name}.dll" with nothing after it, so the game went down inside that plugin's start-up.
verdict.diedLoadingNoReport: The game's own crash reporter wrote no report for it, which is common for a crash this early in start-up.
verdict.winUnknown: Windows recorded the crash but could not name a module: the game jumped to an address where no code was loaded. That is what a call into code that has moved or been unloaded looks like.
ev.diedLoading: log stops at "Loading plugin … {name}.dll", nothing after it
suspect.diedLoading: The game went down while this plugin was starting: RED4ext's log stops at "Loading plugin … {name}.dll".
rule.rs25.title: {mod} was written for an older game version, and it keeps every script mod from loading
rule.rs25.detail: redscript could not compile it. Game update 2.5 added a parameter to InventoryItemModeLogicController.{method}, and {mod} still hooks the old version without it. While one script fails to compile, redscript loads none of them, so all your redscript mods are off until this is fixed. Update {mod} to a version made for 2.5, or remove it until there is one. What redscript wrote:
update.fw.updatedSince: {name} was installed or updated after the game last ran ({date}), so what the logs said then is about the old file.
update.fw.notReached: {name} never got its turn: the game went down while RED4ext was still loading plugins.
